justification: Full independent technical pass, including re-fetching dotnet/runtime source directly (not trusting the article's transcriptions) and re-running every quantitative claim from scratch. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/data-structures/hash-tables.md` from PowerShell: PASS, blocks=23 executed=11, identical on all 3 runs -- no flakiness. I fetched Dictionary.cs, HashHelpers.cs (path is actually src/libraries/Common/src/System/Collections/HashHelpers.cs, not under System.Private.CoreLib as the article's source list implies, but the article never claims a specific path, only cites the GitHub file, so this is not an error), Marvin.cs and NonRandomizedStringEqualityComparer.cs from the dotnet/runtime main branch myself and checked every structural claim against the literal source: `private int[]? _buckets;` and `private Entry[]? _entries;` match exactly (Dictionary.cs lines 26-27); the `Entry` struct's four fields (`hashCode`, `next`, `key`, `value`) match exactly (lines 1871-1881), including the source's own comment confirming `next` is 0-based with -1 as end-of-chain; every one of the ~20 occurrences of the '1-based bucket' comment in the source confirms `_buckets` is 1-based as the article states; the insertion code `entry.next = bucket - 1; ... bucket = index + 1;` (lines 622-625) is exactly the LIFO head-insertion the article describes and diagrams in Figure 2; the resize trigger `if (count == entries.Length) { Resize(); }` (line 610) matches the article's 'count == entries.Length, an effective load factor of 1.0' claim exactly; and `FindValue` (line 397 onward) does exactly the two-step check the article describes -- `entry.hashCode == hashCode && comparer.Equals(entry.key, key)` -- hash compared first, Equals only on a hash match. I traced the prime-growth mechanism through the actual source rather than trusting the article's numbers: `HashHelpers.ExpandPrime` computes `newSize = 2 * oldSize` and `GetPrime(newSize)` returns the smallest table prime >= newSize from the real table `3, 7, 11, 17, 23, 29, 37, 47, 59, 71, 89, 107, 131, 163, 197, 239, 293, 353, 431, ...`; hand-tracing 3->(6->7)->(14->17)->(34->37)->(74->89)->(178->197)->(394->431) reproduces the article's claimed sequence exactly, explaining why it skips 11/23/29/47/59/71/107/131/163/239/293/353 (those are smaller than the doubled threshold at each step, not because the article invented a shorter list). I then independently re-ran this live: a fresh, differently-written C# program (not copied from the article) that adds 250 items to a real `Dictionary<int,int>` and reads `.Capacity` after each change reproduced, on this machine (.NET SDK 10.0.401), the exact sequence 3, 7, 17, 37, 89, 197, 431 the article reports -- fully confirmed, not fabricated. I independently re-ran the mutable-key bug with a different class name and field (`Box.N` instead of `Point.X/Y`) and got exactly the claimed behavior: `ContainsKey`/`TryGetValue`/`Remove` all return false after mutating a stored key's field, while `Count` still reports 1 and `foreach` enumeration still yields the orphaned entry -- this is a real, reproducible characteristic of chained hashing with a mutated hash code, not a contrived one-off. I independently re-ran the worst-case benchmark, both as the article's own exact code (twice, getting ratios of 3272x and 3377x on this machine) and as a from-scratch program against the real `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` (ratio 1421x) -- all three runs land in the same order of magnitude (thousands of times slower for an all-hashcode-1 key set vs. well-distributed keys), confirming the mechanism and direction of the claim are real; the article's own stated '~2,500x' is consistent with that range and is properly hedged as 'on this machine' with the exact nanosecond values wildcarded in the output block, matching EDITORIAL_BRIEF rule 2 rather than overclaiming a fixed universal ratio. Marvin32's per-process crypto-random seed is confirmed: `Marvin.DefaultSeed` is a static property computed once via `GenerateSeed()`, which calls `Interop.GetRandomBytes` (the OS CSPRNG); `String.GetHashCode()` in String.Comparison.cs reads `Marvin.DefaultSeed` and feeds it to `Marvin.ComputeHash32`. The NonRandomizedStringEqualityComparer collision-threshold switch is confirmed verbatim: Dictionary.cs's `if (!typeof(TKey).IsValueType && collisionCount > HashHelpers.HashCollisionThreshold && comparer is NonRandomizedStringEqualityComparer) { Resize(entries.Length, true); }` sits directly under the exact source comment the article quotes word for word ('If we hit the collision threshold we'll need to switch to the comparer which is using randomized string hashing i.e. EqualityComparer<string>.Default.'). Every GetHashCode/Equals contract quotation was checked word-for-word against the live Microsoft Learn pages: 'Two objects that are equal return hash codes that are equal. However, the reverse is not true...', 'If two objects compare as equal, the GetHashCode() method for each object must return the same value... The GetHashCode() method for an object must consistently return the same hash code as long as there is no modification to the object state that determines the return value of the object's Equals method', 'you might think that the mutable object is lost in the hash table', 'two subsequent runs of the same program may return different hash codes', and the Dictionary<TKey,TValue> remark 'As long as an object is used as a key in the Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, it must not change in any way that affects its hash value' -- all confirmed present and accurate on the cited pages, none clipped out of context. The Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.Capacity property is confirmed getter-only and moniker-restricted to net-9.0/net-10.0/net-11.0, matching the article's 'public since .NET 9' claim exactly. Comparing against two real published sources for the likely target query ('C# hash table' / 'how Dictionary works'): GeeksforGeeks's hash-table page and TutorialsTeacher's C# Dictionary tutorial were both fetched and confirmed to contain none of the BCL-source-verified content this article leads with (buckets/entries layout, prime growth measured live, the mutable-key bug, Marvin32/NonRandomizedStringEqualityComparer) -- the differentiation claim in CONTENT_PLAN's premise for this article holds up against real competing pages, not just an assumption. The one open item is the writer's own flagged uncertainty about CLRS 4th edition's chapter numbering for Hash Tables: I confirmed chapter 11 = 'Hash Tables' for the 3rd edition via a CLRS solutions reference site, but could not independently confirm the chapter number specifically for the 4th edition -- MIT Press's own page returned 403 to automated fetches, several 4th-edition-specific TOC sources 404'd, and the web search budget for this session was exhausted before a definitive 4th-edition source was found. I found no evidence the article's 'chapter 11' claim is wrong (CLRS's early-chapter numbering, including the Part III data-structures chapters, is widely cited unchanged between the 3rd and 4th editions), but I also could not positively confirm it myself, so this is an unresolved sourcing-confidence gap rather than a proven error -- it does not trigger the brief's factual-error cap, but it is exactly the kind of unverifiable specific the brief's rule 3 (name the chapter, not a detail you cannot verify) asks to be avoided when it cannot be pinned down. No other factual error was found anywhere in the article: the pigeonhole-principle collision argument, the load-factor/expected-chain-length reasoning, the amortized-resize argument, the struct-key copy-semantics exercise, and the BuggyMap GetHashCode-only exercise are all correct and idiomatic. This keeps the article well clear of the factual-error cap; it is not a 9.5+ only because of the one unresolved (not incorrect, just unconfirmed) CLRS-edition citation.
